target: No solo canta, sino que también baila.
english: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.
tip: Two buts: pero merely contrasts; sino corrects a negative. After 'no solo' it must be sino – and before a full verb like 'baila' it grows a que: 'sino que también'.

target: Sea cual sea el destino, lo importante es disfrutar del camino.
english: Whatever the destination, the important thing is to enjoy the journey.
tip: 'Sea cual sea' is literally 'be it which it be' – Spanish wraps the unknown destino in a doubled subjunctive where English gets away with one word: whatever.

target: Si no recuerdo mal, quedamos a las siete en la plaza.
english: If I remember correctly, we agreed to meet at seven in the square.
tip: 'Quedamos' here isn't 'we stayed' – quedar also means to arrange to meet. 'Quedamos a las siete' = we're on for seven; it's the standard verb for making social plans.

target: No me cabe en la cabeza que haya hecho algo así.
english: I can't wrap my head around him doing something like that (lit. it doesn't fit in my head).
tip: Shock is spatial in Spanish: 'no me cabe en la cabeza' uses caber, to fit – the outrageous idea literally will not fit inside your head.

target: Si me hubiera levantado antes, habría llegado puntual.
english: If I had gotten up earlier, I would have arrived on time.
tip: English 'if I would have' leaks into Spanish as 'si habría' – banned. Si never takes the conditional: 'si me hubiera levantado' sets the unreal past, 'habría llegado' gives the result.

target: Aunque hubiera tenido más tiempo, el resultado habría sido el mismo.
english: Even if I had had more time, the result would have been the same.
tip: Aunque plays two roles: with hubiera it means 'even IF' (never happened); with plain indicative it's 'even though' (fact). 'Aunque hubiera tenido más tiempo' – that time never existed.

target: Cabe mencionar que la catedral data del siglo quince.
english: It's worth mentioning that the cathedral dates from the fifteenth century.
tip: Caber means 'to fit', so 'cabe mencionar' is literally 'there's room to mention it' – the polished Spanish move for slipping in a fact worth noting.
'Buenas noches' works coming and going – good evening as a hello after dark, good night as a farewell. One phrase, both directions.
'De nada' = literally 'of nothing' – you owe me nothing, it was nothing. That's the logic inside the Spanish you're-welcome.
Languages go lowercase: 'inglés', never Inglés. Nationalities and days too – Spanish capitalizes far less than English.
In Spain waiters won't bring the bill until you ask – lingering after a meal is normal, not a hint to leave. Say 'la cuenta, por favor', or mime signing in the air.
Why plural? 'Buenos días' wishes you good DAYS – likely from the old blessing 'may God give you good days.' All the time-of-day greetings stay plural.
